timeline.title: Born near Bukhara
timeline.text: Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah ibn Sina was born in the village of Afshana, near Bukhara. Wikipedia gives about 980; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy says the 970s, perhaps as early as 964. His father, from Balkh, worked for the Samanid rulers.

timeline.title: The Quran by heart
timeline.text: The family moved to Bukhara, a center of learning. A teacher taught him the Quran and Arabic literature, and by about age ten he knew the whole Quran by heart and amazed those around him.

timeline.title: Outgrowing his teacher
timeline.text: His father brought a tutor named al-Natili into the house to teach him logic. The boy soon solved questions better than his master. He went on alone through Euclid's geometry and Ptolemy's astronomy. The exact year is not recorded; this was in his early teens.

timeline.title: A doctor at sixteen
timeline.text: He turned to medicine and found it "not difficult". After learning from books he began to visit the sick, and by sixteen other physicians were coming to study with him.

timeline.title: Physician to the ruler
timeline.text: When the Samanid ruler Nuh II fell ill, the young Ibn Sina was called to help treat him. As a reward he was allowed into the royal library, with rooms of chests full of books, some he never saw again anywhere. Wikipedia puts this at age 17; Browne says he was a little over 18.

timeline.title: Forty readings and a cheap book
timeline.text: He read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times and knew it by heart without understanding it. Then a bookseller talked him into buying a small book by al-Farabi for three dirhams, and the meaning became clear. He gave to the poor the next day in thanks.

timeline.title: The library burns
timeline.text: The royal library later burned down. His enemies claimed he had set the fire so that only he would hold its knowledge. Browne, writing in 1921, reports this as a claim by his detractors; there is no evidence for it. The year of the fire is not recorded.

timeline.title: His first books
timeline.text: At about 21 he began to write, often at the request of neighbours. For one, Abu al-Husayn al-Arudi, he wrote a general book of philosophy named after him. His first work, the Compendium on the Soul, also dates from his youth.

timeline.title: His father dies
timeline.text: His father died when he was 21 or 22; sources disagree. Ibn Sina took up government posts, but the fall of the Samanid state soon forced him to leave Bukhara.

timeline.title: To the court of Khwarazm
timeline.text: He moved to Gurganj and served its ruler Ali ibn Mamun. The date is uncertain: one encyclopedia puts the move in 999, and Wikipedia gives a range from about 997 to 1009.

timeline.title: No country had room for him
timeline.text: He left Gurganj and travelled through Nasa, Baward and Tus to Gorgan, hoping for the patronage of its learned ruler Qabus. But Qabus had been overthrown and died. Ibn Sina fell seriously ill on the road and wrote a sad verse about having no buyer for his worth.

timeline.title: A lifelong student
timeline.text: In Gorgan he met Abu Ubayd al-Juzjani, who became his student and companion for the rest of his life. Ibn Sina told him the story of his early years, and al-Juzjani later finished it. It is the main source for his life.

timeline.title: Physician at Ray
timeline.text: He entered the service of the young ruler Majd al-Dawla and his mother Sayyida Shirin at Ray, near modern Tehran, and treated the ruler for melancholia.

timeline.title: The Book of Healing begins
timeline.text: He most likely began The Book of Healing (al-Shifa) around 1014. It became a huge encyclopedia of logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics.

timeline.title: Vizier of Hamadan
timeline.text: In Hamadan he won a public debate and soon became vizier, the chief minister, of the ruler Shams al-Dawla. By day he worked for the state; much of the night he taught students and dictated his books.

timeline.title: Dismissed, then recalled
timeline.text: Soldiers mutinied against him and he was dismissed and held for a time. When Shams al-Dawla fell ill again, he called Ibn Sina back, apologized and gave him his post again. The exact year is not recorded.

timeline.title: The Book of Healing completed
timeline.text: He finished The Book of Healing around 1020, writing at the home of a friend. It was published around 1027.

timeline.title: Hiding and prison
timeline.text: After Shams al-Dawla died in 1021, Ibn Sina refused to stay on under the new ruler and went into hiding. He was found and held for about four months in the fortress of Fardajan. There he is said to have written his famous floating man thought experiment and the allegory Hayy ibn Yaqzan.

timeline.title: Calm years in Isfahan
timeline.text: He went to Isfahan and served its ruler Ala al-Dawla, probably from about 1024; the year is uncertain. These were the most settled years of his life. For his patron he wrote the Danishnama, a book of philosophy in Persian.

timeline.title: The Canon of Medicine
timeline.text: He began the Canon in Gurganj, carried it on at Ray, and completed it by about 1025. Sources disagree on exactly when and where it was finished. Its five books cover the basics of medicine, medicines one by one, diseases of each part of the body, illnesses of the whole body, and compound remedies.

timeline.title: The Book of Healing is published
timeline.text: The Book of Healing was published around 1027. He later wrote The Book of Salvation (al-Najat), a shorter version of its teaching.

timeline.title: On the move again
timeline.text: In January 1030, when the army of Mahmud of Ghazni occupied Isfahan, he moved to Khuzistan for about two months. After returning he began Pointers and Reminders, one of his last great books.

timeline.title: Watching the sky
timeline.text: He claimed to have seen Venus pass across the face of the Sun in 1032. Modern scholars doubt he could have seen it; he may have seen a sunspot instead.

timeline.title: Death in Hamadan
timeline.text: While travelling with Ala al-Dawla he fell seriously ill with colic. He died in Hamadan on 22 June 1037 and was buried there. Wikipedia gives his age as 56 or 57; Browne gives 58, probably counting lunar years. Worn out by hard work, he had carried on writing to the end.

timeline.title: An early copy survives
timeline.text: The earliest known copy of the fifth volume of the Canon is dated 1052, only 15 years after his death. It is now kept in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto.

timeline.title: The Canon in print
timeline.text: A Latin translation of the Canon had been made in Spain in the 1100s or 1200s; sources disagree on whether Gerard of Cremona or a later translator made it. The first printed edition appeared in 1472, and the Canon was taught in European universities for centuries, in Padua as late as 1715.

timeline.title: A new mausoleum
timeline.text: A new tomb designed by the architect Hooshang Seyhoun was dedicated in Hamadan in May 1954, to mark the thousandth anniversary of his birth. It includes a small museum and a library.

works.title: The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb)
works.text: A medical encyclopedia in five books, from general principles to diseases and remedies. Book 2 sets out rules for testing new drugs. In Latin it was a standard textbook in European universities for centuries.

works.title: The Book of Healing (al-Shifa)
works.text: His largest work: an encyclopedia of logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics, begun around 1014 and finished around 1020. It includes ideas about how mountains form.

works.title: The Book of Salvation (al-Najat)
works.text: A shorter version of the teaching in The Book of Healing, written after it and drawn from his earlier writings; the exact year is not known.

works.title: Pointers and Reminders (al-Isharat wa al-Tanbihat)
works.text: One of his last great summaries of philosophy, begun after 1030 and written in a brief, hinting style.

works.title: Danishnama-yi Alai (Book of Knowledge for Ala al-Dawla)
works.text: His main work in Persian, his native language, covering logic, metaphysics and music theory, written for his patron in Isfahan.

works.title: A Compendium on the Soul
works.text: His first work, written in his youth for the Samanid ruler; the exact year is not known. An English translation by Edward Abbott Van Dyck (1906) is free on Project Gutenberg.

works.title: Philosophy for Arudi
works.text: Written at about 21 for a neighbour who asked for a general book of learning; his first full summary of philosophy.

works.title: The floating man
works.text: A thought experiment: a person created floating in the air, with no senses working, would still know that he exists. Ibn Sina used it to argue that the self is not the same as the body.

works.title: Hayy ibn Yaqzan
works.text: A short philosophical allegory, written during his imprisonment. Its title was later borrowed by Ibn Tufail for a famous novel.

works.title: On the Science of the Pulse
works.text: A short treatise in Persian, in nine chapters, dedicated to Ala al-Dawla, so probably written after he moved to Isfahan.

works.title: The Life, told to al-Juzjani
works.text: His own account of his early years, given to his student al-Juzjani, who added the rest of his life after his death. It is the main source for his biography.
